name: Karl Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign, and what you tell me is confidential. I'd like to hear what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What does an ordinary day at work involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage five people buying building maintenance services for a large hotel group. We compare bids for lifts, boilers and fire doors, check the terms and go to a hotel when a contractor says the work is finished. I'm 27, have an MBA and have got good at spotting when a low bid has simply left a required inspection out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part do you like, and what is weighing on you now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like shaking the engineer's hand after a lift is working again; a contract should mean something in the actual building. I spend too much time in email, though, and I have never used an AI tool because I don't trust a summary to carry a safety clause. My fiancée Leena teaches music at a school, and we're saving for a modest wedding next year. I have about three months of expenses put by, earn a normal manager's wage and could find some similar offices nearby if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little automation of routine paperwork would not surprise me. The hotel still needs someone to compare a contract with the work on site, and I know the contractors. But a flat year doesn't make the wedding or rent cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to keep reading the service records before signing a contractor's invoice. I'd tell friends a shortcut on email doesn't fix a broken lift. I wouldn't say AI is useless; it can file things if a person checks them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel steady at work, but I'm guarding the wedding account. The hotel group is asking everyone to hold costs, and a three-month reserve doesn't let me ignore that. I have some nearby offices to try if this one stalls, though I'd rather keep the job I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this week I'd keep the monthly on-site check of fire doors and lift records with my team, and make the contractor sign each missing item. Through the first year of a plateau I'd stay in this role, put 150 a month toward the wedding while Leena's wage covers her share of rent, and leave the three-month emergency fund alone. If costs rise, we'd shrink the reception before touching that reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the work, less calm about the bills. I can picture the wedding without picturing a job loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take off the wedding bill first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hired car. My brother can drive us to the wedding, and nobody will remember how we arrived. I wouldn't skip the meal for our families; that is the part that matters to Leena and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI can file things. Why don't you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know where my clauses are in the contract binder. Learning a new system just to find the same page has not appealed to me. If the firm shows me a safe one for filing, I might look, but I haven't opened one yet.

say: Keep the **site checks** before signing invoices for lift and fire-door work.
AI might file emails, but a **broken lift** needs a contractor to fix it.
think: My **job feels steady**, though the group is holding costs.
The **wedding budget** needs care even with three months saved.
do: Keep **monthly on-site checks** and get contractors to sign missing items.
Put **150 monthly** toward the wedding while Leena covers her rent share.
Cut the **hired car** if costs rise before using emergency savings.
feel: I feel **steady** about work, with ordinary bill worries.
S0.quote: My brother can drive us to the wedding, and nobody will remember how we arrived.
fieldNote: His **contract binder** and known contractors anchor his confidence in the plateau picture.
Wedding spending is **conditional on rent**, and he guards three months of emergency savings.
He is open to AI filing eventually but **has not used it** yet.

steps.text: Keep monthly site checks for lift and fire-door contractors
Drop the hired wedding car if costs rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing tenders, checking bids and planning service visits fill most of our week. If software takes that first, one manager could cover several hotels and my five-person team could be smaller. The contractor still has to repair the lift, but that isn't the job I'm paid to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to mark every safety term before anyone accepts a machine's comparison of bids. To friends I'd say firms are free to buy a better tool, but they owe staff an honest timetable. I would not call a cheaper contract a saving if the inspection has vanished from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the lead role even though I know the buildings better than most. My director may keep me to inspect work, but she could just as easily centralise everything and send someone else. Leena's teaching wage covers her part of rent, not both parts, so I'd feel a cut quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd list the clauses that led to rejected bids last year and ask the director which duties she expects to automate. If a bid-comparison pilot starts next year, I'd check its first ten tenders by hand against the signed contracts before using its findings. I'd stop the weekly restaurant meal and add that money to the emergency fund while the staffing decision is unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, because this is the work I know. I'd rather have an awkward talk with the director than hear about a cut through a calendar invite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test a tool you have never used?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with our finance analyst while she runs it and bring the paper contract. I could compare ten results without pretending to know the software. If I find it missed a fire-door inspection, I'll say exactly where.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your team if you suspect cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what the director actually said, not a rumour. I can't promise jobs I don't control. I can give each person the record of the contracts they've handled if they need to apply elsewhere.

say: Mark **safety terms** before accepting an automatic bid comparison.
Firms can change tools but owe staff an **honest timetable**.
think: My **lead role could go** even with strong knowledge of the buildings.
Leena's pay covers **her rent share**, not the whole household.
do: List **rejected-bid clauses** and ask which duties the director may automate.
Check the first **ten pilot tenders** by hand against signed terms.
Stop **weekly restaurant meals** and add the money to emergency savings.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the role and about telling the team.
S1.quote: I would not call a cheaper contract a saving if the inspection has vanished from it.
fieldNote: His **hands-on contract checks** are still office judgment work exposed to stronger AI.
He will test a pilot **through a finance colleague**, without claiming he already uses AI.
He thinks firms may change but owes workers an **honest timetable**.

steps.text: Check ten pilot tenders against signed contracts before trusting comparisons
Stop the weekly restaurant meal while staffing is unclear
Put the restaurant savings into the emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it can do nearly all thinking work in 2028, bid comparisons and contract calls are both exposed. I can't defend my desk by saying I know every hotel's lift when the system can learn that too. The actual lifting and repair may wait until robots around 2031, but I am a contract manager, not a lift engineer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my people the date on the card and ask for a written plan for the contracts department. I'd tell Leena we may have to change the wedding date, and I'd say so privately to family before invitations go out. I would not claim a human signature means five human managers stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my role to disappear or lose much of its pay after 2028. Three months saved and Leena's teaching wage would cover part of our bills, not my whole salary. There are some similar employers nearby, but their contract desks could be changing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month Leena and I would pause the wedding venue deposit and put the planned payment into cash. I'd ask the hotel operations director whether a paid building inspection opening exists and request its wage and duties in writing; I wouldn't call it a safe move because its reports could also change in 2028. If AGI arrives and my job ends, I'd apply only if that opening still exists and the pay covers my share of rent; otherwise I'd use our reserve for a wider job search while Leena keeps teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wake up already thinking about the venue bill, and this would add a job loss to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an inspection post without training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd ask to shadow an inspector on company time and have someone show me the fire-door checks before I signed a report. Physical checks may last until 2031, but the planning and paperwork could go with AGI in 2028. I'd need to know what I was actually being hired to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leena's parents about the delayed wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are keeping the marriage plan and postponing the venue payment until we know my job. I won't ask my fiancée's family to finance a party because I lost wages. My brother can still help us arrange a smaller day later.

say: Ask for a **written contracts plan** before promising the team job safety.
Tell our families about a possible **wedding delay** before invitations go out.
think: My **contract role may disappear** soon after 2028.
Three months saved and Leena's wage cover **some bills**, not my salary.
do: Pause the **venue deposit** now and keep that cash.
Ask for a **paid inspection vacancy** with its wage and duties in writing.
Take **inspection work** after company-time shadowing only with demonstrated checks, a live vacancy, and pay covering my rent share.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely salary loss alongside the wedding bill.
S2.quote: I won't ask my fiancée's family to finance a party because I lost wages.
fieldNote: He sees **2028 as desk risk** and recognises inspection reports could change then too.
Physical inspection may last until **2031 robots**, but he has no training or guaranteed opening.
A venue deposit is the **first payment paused**, while Leena's income remains limited support.

steps.text: Pause the wedding venue deposit before invitations go out
Take inspection work after company-time shadowing only with a live vacancy and rent-covering wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me find out whether I can do the actual building checks, instead of waving an MBA at a tradesman. Contract planning still faces AGI in 2031; physical checks of doors and lifts may need people until robots arrive around 2034. I can't assume a hotel keeps an inspection manager just because it keeps an inspector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that there is time to make individual plans while our pay continues. At home I'd say Leena and I can keep the wedding simple and still learn where work is going. I'd rather ask a contractor what skill is needed than sell everyone a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might move into a paid inspection role if I can learn the checks properly and one actually opens. I'd be less frightened with five years to add to our savings, but I would still lose the office title I've worked for. I don't know whether I'd enjoy that trade every day, so I should try it before promising a switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd request a paid shadow day each month with the fire-door inspector, and if approved I'd complete the visits and learn the checklist under supervision. Leena and I would keep the wedding small and add 200 monthly to our emergency account while both wages hold. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for a posted on-site inspection job only if the wage covers our bills; if no such job opens, I'd use the reserve to search the nearby hotel groups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steadier. Five years is enough to test my hands, not only my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do on the first shadow day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the inspector close each fire door and record whether the seal catches, then compare it with the maintenance order. I would not sign the safety certificate until qualified. A fire-door inspector's job is something someone has to show me, not a page in a business book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm will not pay for the shadow time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my contract post and ask a contractor if a paid trainee opening comes up. I won't spend the wedding fund on an unpaid promise. If there is no paid route, I'd look for another contract office while those jobs still exist.

say: Use the years of wages to make **individual work plans**.
Ask a contractor about **real skills and openings** before paying for a course.
think: I could take **paid inspection work** if training and a post exist.
The loss of my office title still **stings**, even with more preparation time.
do: Complete **monthly paid shadow visits** if the firm approves them.
Add **200 monthly** to emergency savings while both wages hold.
Apply for a **posted inspection role** after 2031 only if wages cover bills.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but with time to test a supervised route.
S3.quote: A fire-door inspector's job is something someone has to show me, not a page in a business book.
fieldNote: He will learn **physical checks under supervision**, without claiming an MBA qualifies him to sign certificates.
He distinguishes **2031 contract work** from later robot exposure of on-site checks.
The plan protects the **wedding fund** unless there is a paid route into inspections.

steps.text: Complete monthly paid fire-door shadow visits if approved by the firm
Add 200 monthly to emergency savings while both wages continue
Apply for a posted inspection role after 2031 only at affordable wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade lets us get married, build more cash and see whether a real trade fits me. The contract work could still go to AGI by 2036, while hands-on inspections face robots around 2039. I would be 37; I don't want to be 37 with only a title and no skill I can show at a building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger managers to seek paid apprenticeships and site time while the company needs them. I'd say families can help each other, but a firm that benefits from a trained worker should pay for the training. I wouldn't tell someone to quit for a certificate with no job behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish an inspection qualification and earn a wage checking buildings if my company funds it or a contractor pays me as a trainee. Leena and I could be settled by then, perhaps with a home deposit saved, but I won't count on a house I haven't bought. Even an inspector's reporting work could shrink in 2036, and the physical checks face 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask the hotel group to sponsor a fire safety inspection course with paid site hours, and if they approve I'd finish the course and supervised checks before signing anything myself. We'd keep putting 200 monthly into a house deposit after the wedding as long as rent and emergency savings stay covered. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd seek a posted inspection job at the hotels or a contractor only if the wage works; I'd keep the deposit in cash if the offer is uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More at ease, though not entirely. A real qualification and a saved deposit give us choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you ask the firm to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They get a worker who knows their buildings and their contractors. Apprenticeship is an exchange: time and wages for skill and dependable work. I don't want a public cheque for a course the hotel group can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no sponsored place in 2027?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on contracts and ask again when a place opens, while visiting sites with qualified staff where I'm allowed. I would not charge the course to our wedding account. Leena and I could still save for a home more slowly.

say: Managers should seek **paid site training** while firms still need them.
Families can help, but **employers should fund** useful apprenticeships.
think: A funded qualification might lead to **inspection wages** before 2036.
Even physical inspections could face **2039 robots**; a house remains a hope, not an asset.
do: Finish a **sponsored inspection course** if the hotel group approves in 2027.
Save **200 monthly** for a home after the wedding if essentials stay covered.
Seek a **posted inspection opening** after 2036 only if the wage works.
feel: I feel **more at ease**, with choices but no guaranteed inspection job.
S4.quote: Apprenticeship is an exchange: time and wages for skill and dependable work.
fieldNote: His **traditional work view** favours paid apprenticeship and family support over a public cheque.
The course requires **employer sponsorship**, and he would not raid wedding money if refused.
He keeps **2036 office exposure** separate from possible loss of physical inspection work around 2039.

steps.text: Complete a sponsored fire safety inspection course if approved in 2027
Save 200 monthly for a home after the wedding if rent and emergency savings stay covered
Apply for a posted inspection job after 2036 only if wages cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My best skill is remembering what a contractor promised and what a building actually needs, but a system that can reason through the whole contract could take the office part quickly. A dated notice, a paid opening in building inspection and enough wage to keep paying our rent would help. I'd also want Leena and me to choose the wedding date ourselves, not have a layoff choose it for us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will stand in front of the hotel manager when the repaired lift stops again. A contract can be written by anything, but somebody still owes the guest an answer. I know that answer might take fewer managers than we have now.

headlineQuote: A contract can be written by anything, but somebody still owes the guest an answer.
portrait: Karl, **27**, leads five people buying maintenance work for a large hotel group and checks whether contractors fulfil safety terms.
His **MBA and strong record** support his judgment, though he has never used AI tools and prefers direct inspections.
He and his **fiancée Leena** have three months saved and plan a modest wedding while living on typical manager pay.
He fears **AGI by 2028** could remove contract work before he finds an affordable on-site role; longer warning lets him train cautiously.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take his contract role before he secures a paid inspection opening.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated notice** and a real paid building inspection vacancy with wages that cover rent.
Time to choose the **wedding date** with Leena before any layoff forces the decision.
